units.name: Rotavirus Wave
units.ability: Fast wave that drains hydration (NSP4 enterotoxin, villus damage). Antibiotics are useless against a virus.
units.weak: ORS (zinc for children under 5); IgA; rotavirus vaccine roughly halves severe attacks but does not stop all attacks

units.name: ETEC Swarm
units.ability: Many small units; heat-labile and heat-stable toxins drain hydration.
units.weak: ORS; antibiotics usually not needed (azithromycin only for severe traveller's diarrhoea)

units.name: Cholera Flood
units.ability: Cholera toxin (cAMP rise, chloride secretion) drains hydration very fast; little direct damage. Very acid-sensitive.
units.weak: ORS, with IV Ringer's lactate for severe dehydration; single-dose doxycycline (azithromycin alternative) for moderate-severe cases; oral cholera vaccine (about 65%, 3-5 years)

units.name: Shigella Raider
units.ability: Invades the colon epithelium (double damage to colon walls; bacillary dysentery is a colitis). Kills macrophages by pyroptosis (double damage to Macrophage Towers). Acid-tolerant: 10-100 bacteria can infect.
units.weak: Azithromycin or ceftriaxone; neutrophils. Never Stop-Flow (loperamide). Ciprofloxacin often fails in India (resistance).

units.name: Typhoid Stalker
units.ability: Crosses the gut wall through Peyer's patches, survives inside macrophages and heads for the liver and blood. Fluoroquinolone resistance is common in India.
units.weak: Ceftriaxone or azithromycin (fluoroquinolones usually fail in India); Kupffer cells; macrophages only after T-cell activation; typhoid conjugate vaccine (about 80% protection, not lifelong)

units.name: Amoeba Blob
units.ability: Slow; squeezes through walls and heads for the liver gate, where it does double damage (amoebic liver abscess). Lyses neutrophils. When killed it leaves a cyst behind unless a luminal agent clears it.
units.weak: Metronidazole for the invasive trophozoite, then a luminal agent (diloxanide furoate or paromomycin) for the cysts; activated macrophages; Kupffer cells

units.name: Amoeba Cyst
units.ability: Left behind when an Amoeba Blob dies. Cysts sit in the gut lumen behind a tough wall: immune cells and tissue drugs barely touch them, so the infection relapses unless a luminal agent clears them.

units.name: H. pylori Driller
units.ability: Urease neutralises acid, so the Acid Moat cannot hurt it. Drills the stomach (double damage there, half elsewhere) and evades immune cells.
units.weak: Combination therapy only: PPI + two antibiotics together. A single antibiotic alone breeds resistance.

units.name: Candida Creeper
units.ability: Cannot be deployed. Overgrows when broad-spectrum antibiotics wipe out the gut flora; with no healthy flora it is 60% stronger. Healthy flora kills it (colonisation resistance).
units.weak: Rebuilding the Gut Flora Garden and stopping the culprit antibiotic. Candida in stool is usually colonisation: antifungals are for thrush or invasive candidiasis, not for gut Candida after antibiotics.

units.name: Worm Titan
units.ability: Big slow tank that steals nutrients while it lives in the intestine; barely moved by peristalsis.

units.name: C. diff Phantom
units.ability: Cannot be deployed. Appears when broad-spectrum antibiotics destroy the defender's gut flora (toxins A and B, pseudomembranous colitis).
units.weak: Oral fidaxomicin or vancomycin (metronidazole only if neither is available); stop the culprit antibiotic; rebuild the flora; never loperamide

drugs.name: H. pylori regimen (L1-2: PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin; L3+: bismuth quadruple)

buildings.name: Bone Marrow Core
buildings.desc: Source of all immune cells. Headquarters: its level unlocks other buildings and raises storage and army size. Destroying it is a star.

buildings.name: Acid Moat
buildings.desc: Gastric acid damages every germ in the stomach. Strong against acid-sensitive cholera; weak against acid-tolerant Shigella; useless against H. pylori (urease). PPIs weaken it.

buildings.name: Mucus Wall
buildings.desc: Mucus layer from goblet cells. Cheap wall; sticky mucus reduces the damage germs do to it.

buildings.name: Villi Wall
buildings.desc: Small-intestine epithelium with tight junctions. Strong wall, but toxin germs nearby make it leak fluid (extra hydration loss).

buildings.name: Gut Flora Garden
buildings.desc: Normal microbiota: a living colon wall (colonisation resistance) that regrows when antibiotics stop and boosts nutrients. While healthy it kills C. difficile and Candida in the colon. Broad-spectrum antibiotic fire damages it; if it dies after antibiotic damage, C. difficile and Candida appear.

buildings.name: Paneth Cell Tower
buildings.desc: Defensins from small-intestinal crypts. Rapid fire against bacteria.

buildings.name: IgA Antibody Cannon
buildings.desc: Secretory IgA from plasma cells. Long range; neutralises toxins (hit germs drain less); double damage against germs the base is vaccinated against.

buildings.name: Macrophage Tower
buildings.desc: Lamina propria macrophages engulf germs. Typhoid survives inside resting macrophages until T cells activate them (interferon-gamma); Shigella kills macrophages by pyroptosis.

buildings.name: Neutrophil Reserve
buildings.desc: Releases a neutrophil swarm that hits every germ in range. Key defence against Shigella (the pus cells of dysentery) and Candida; weak against Typhoid and Amoeba (amoebae lyse neutrophils).

buildings.name: Kupffer Cell Gate
buildings.desc: Liver macrophages on the portal route: a gate that blocks every germ, with triple strength against Typhoid and Amoeba. Last line before the blood.

buildings.name: Peristalsis Conveyor
buildings.desc: Gut movement flushes germs out of the body (diarrhoea is partly a defence): regular flush damage to every free-floating germ in the small intestine. Invasive germs attached to the wall take half. Stop-Flow (loperamide) switches it off.

buildings.name: ORS + Zinc Station
buildings.desc: Low-osmolarity ORS refills hydration: the main treatment for watery diarrhoea. It cannot keep up in severe dehydration (below 25% it works at only 20%) - that needs IV fluids. Level 3 adds zinc for children under 5 (less fluid loss).

buildings.name: IV Ringer's Lactate Stand
buildings.desc: Severe dehydration and shock need intravenous Ringer's lactate (WHO Plan C). Switches on automatically when hydration falls below 25% and runs until 50%.

buildings.name: Drug Battery
buildings.desc: Fires one researched drug at the germs it is prescribed for. Strong against susceptible germs, useless (and resistance-breeding) against the rest. Each shot costs ATP. Broad-spectrum drugs damage the gut flora.

buildings.name: Peyer's Patch
buildings.desc: Gut lymphoid tissue. Research T cells here. While it stands, immune memory makes towers stronger against germs the base has beaten before.

buildings.name: Pharmacy Lab
buildings.desc: The formulary: research new drugs and rapid diagnostics.

buildings.name: Vaccine Lab
buildings.desc: Research vaccines that give lasting (but not complete) protection against one germ.

research.name: T helper cells
research.desc: Th1 cells (interferon-gamma) activate macrophages so they kill intracellular Typhoid.

rotavirus.note: Indian rotavirus vaccines prevent roughly half to 60% of severe rotavirus gastroenteritis in infancy; protection is partial and wanes.

typhoid.note: Typhoid conjugate vaccine efficacy about 80% in field trials; protection lasts several years, not for life.

cholera.note: Two-dose killed oral cholera vaccine gives about 65% protection lasting around 3-5 years.

spells.name: Contaminated Water
spells.desc: For 5 seconds every deployment brings one extra germ (faecal-oral spread).

spells.name: Quorum Sensing
spells.desc: Germs near the target coordinate: +40% speed and +30% damage for 6 seconds.

spells.name: Immune Evasion
spells.desc: Germs near the target cannot be targeted by immune cells for 4 seconds (drugs still hit them).

spells.name: Biofilm Dome
spells.desc: A barrier: germs inside take 70% less drug damage and 40% less immune damage for 8 seconds. Biofilms tolerate antibiotics.

campaign.title: Child with watery diarrhoea
campaign.case: Aarav, 14 months, from a Delhi slum: 3 days of watery diarrhoea and vomiting, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly. Stool has no blood. Rotavirus antigen positive.
campaign.best: ORS + zinc only; no antibiotic. Rotavirus vaccine prevents most severe cases.

campaign.title: Traveller's diarrhoea
campaign.case: A 22-year-old exchange student, 4 days after arriving in India, has 5 loose watery stools a day with cramps. No fever, no blood, passing urine normally.
campaign.best: ORS. Antibiotics only if severe (azithromycin); most cases settle on their own.

campaign.title: Cholera outbreak after floods
campaign.case: After monsoon floods in a relief camp, a 30-year-old man has profuse 'rice-water' stools, vomiting and leg cramps. He is drowsy with very sunken eyes. Stool shows darting motile comma-shaped bacteria.
campaign.best: IV Ringer's lactate for severe dehydration, then ORS; a single dose of doxycycline (azithromycin as the alternative) for moderate-to-severe cases; oral cholera vaccine (2 doses) for the camp.

campaign.title: Bacillary dysentery
campaign.case: A 24-year-old engineering student has fever, abdominal cramps, tenesmus and frequent small stools with blood and mucus. He asks the pharmacist for loperamide to 'stop the motions' before an exam.
campaign.best: Azithromycin (ceftriaxone if severe) and ORS. Never antimotility drugs (loperamide) in dysentery. Ciprofloxacin often fails in India because of resistance. Neutrophils, not macrophages, fight Shigella.

campaign.title: Enteric fever
campaign.case: A 19-year-old hostel student has had a step-ladder fever for 9 days, headache, a coated tongue and a relative bradycardia. Blood culture grows Salmonella Typhi resistant to ciprofloxacin.
campaign.best: Ceftriaxone or azithromycin by susceptibility; ciprofloxacin usually fails in India. Protect the liver gate. Typhoid conjugate vaccine protects about 80%, for several years.

campaign.title: Amoebic dysentery and liver abscess
campaign.case: A 35-year-old man had bloody diarrhoea a month ago; now he has fever and right upper abdominal pain with tender hepatomegaly. Ultrasound shows a single liver abscess. Serology for Entamoeba histolytica is positive.
campaign.best: Metronidazole, followed by a luminal agent (paromomycin or diloxanide furoate) to clear the gut cysts. Protect the liver gate.

campaign.title: Peptic ulcer
campaign.case: A 45-year-old man has burning epigastric pain that wakes him at night and improves with food. Endoscopy shows a duodenal ulcer; rapid urease test is positive.
campaign.best: Combination therapy: PPI + two antibiotics together (triple therapy), or bismuth quadruple therapy where clarithromycin resistance is high. One antibiotic alone fails and breeds resistance.

campaign.title: Diarrhoea after broad-spectrum antibiotics
campaign.case: A 68-year-old woman on ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin for 10 days after surgery develops fever, leucocytosis and foul watery diarrhoea. Stool test for C. difficile toxin is positive.
campaign.best: Stop the culprit antibiotics, give oral fidaxomicin or vancomycin (not metronidazole when these are available), rehydrate, and let the flora recover. No loperamide.

campaign.title: School child with worms
campaign.case: A 9-year-old school child is pale and thin, with poor appetite and vague abdominal pain; a round worm was passed in the stool last week. Haemoglobin is 9 g/dL.
campaign.best: Single-dose albendazole 400 mg (200 mg for ages 1-2); National Deworming Day (10 February and 10 August, ages 1-19); iron for anaemia; hand-washing and sanitation.

campaign.title: Boss level: outbreak in a hostel mess
campaign.case: Forty students fall ill within two days after a hostel mess feast: some with watery diarrhoea, some with bloody stools, two with high fever. Water samples show faecal contamination.
campaign.best: Hydration for everyone; the right drug for each germ; no unnecessary antibiotics; vaccination and safe water for the hostel.

matrixLegend.P: Partly effective (often because of resistance in India); exact value per cell in matrixPct
matrixLegend.X: Active against the germ but NOT indicated: does some damage, counts as an unnecessary antibiotic shot
matrixLegend.N: Not effective: the shot is wasted and breeds resistance

matrixNotes.typhoid.fluoroquinolone: Most Salmonella Typhi in India are fluoroquinolone non-susceptible; ciprofloxacin should not be used empirically.
matrixNotes.shigella.fluoroquinolone: Fluoroquinolone resistance in Shigella is common in India.
matrixNotes.etec: Antibiotics are generally not needed; ORS is the treatment. Azithromycin only for severe traveller's diarrhoea.
matrixNotes.hpylori: Clarithromycin, amoxicillin, tetracycline and metronidazole work only inside a full regimen (PPI-based triple therapy or bismuth quadruple therapy); any one alone fails and selects resistance. Azithromycin is not part of any standard regimen.
matrixNotes.cdiff.metronidazole: Metronidazole is no longer recommended for C. difficile; use only if oral vancomycin and fidaxomicin are unavailable (IDSA/SHEA 2021).
matrixNotes.amoeba: Metronidazole kills invasive trophozoites; a luminal agent is still needed to clear cysts and prevent relapse.
matrixNotes.candida.antifungal: Candida in stool after antibiotics is usually colonisation, not infection; antifungals are for thrush or invasive candidiasis.
matrixNotes.cholera: Single-dose doxycycline is first-line (GTFCC 2018, all ages); azithromycin is the alternative.

trials.name: Monsoon diarrhoea clinic
trials.brief: Watery diarrhoea from cholera, ETEC and rotavirus. Rehydrate first; use antibiotics only where they help.

trials.name: Dysentery ward
trials.brief: Bloody diarrhoea from Shigella and Amoeba, on a ward that over-uses ceftriaxone. Choose the right drugs, protect the flora, and never stop the flow.

trials.name: Fever and pain clinic
trials.brief: Enteric fever, a peptic ulcer and a worm load in the same week. Match each germ to its drug.

attack.name: Rapid Replication
attack.desc: Binary fission at full speed: every living germ regains 30% of its health.

attack.name: Quorum Surge
attack.desc: Quorum sensing switches on everywhere: all germs move 40% faster and hit 30% harder for 8 seconds.

attack.name: Capsule Cloak
attack.desc: A polysaccharide capsule hides every germ from immune cells for 6 seconds (drugs still hit).

defence.name: ORS Bolus
defence.desc: A big drink of oral rehydration solution: hydration jumps up by 15% at once.

defence.name: Complement Cascade
defence.desc: Membrane attack complexes punch holes in every germ: each loses 20% of its full health.

defence.name: Secretory IgA Flood
defence.desc: Secretory IgA neutralises toxins: diarrhoea drains much less hydration for 10 seconds.
